contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Use two pointers when the candidate is a relation between selected positions and interior elements are not part of the candidate; use sliding window when the candidate is the contiguous interval and its full contents determine validity or score.

authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring; human review required

items.prompt: A sorted array must yield any two distinct positions whose values add to a target. Values between the two positions are not part of the candidate answer. Which model should drive the first linear-time strategy?

options.text: Use a two-pointers invariant.
Use a sliding-window validity invariant.
Classify it as two pointers solely because two indices appear.

feedback.reason: The candidate is a relation between two selected endpoints, not the interval between them.

blocks.text: Sorted order lets an endpoint comparison rule eliminate impossible pairs: a sum that is too small moves the lower endpoint, and a sum that is too large moves the higher endpoint. The elements between the endpoints are merely unexamined candidates; they are not maintained as one aggregate object. A sliding window would instead interpret every element from left through right as part of the current candidate and would need a validity or score rule for that entire range. The transfer test is therefore about the answer object, not the variable names: two selected positions support a pair relation, while a contiguous block whose interior matters supports a window.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sliding_window: This is plausible because the endpoints enclose a range, but the enclosed values are not maintained or scored. A window becomes appropriate only when the whole contiguous range is the candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.indices_only: Two indices are necessary here but are not the reason for the classification. The decisive evidence is the pair relation plus the sorted-order elimination rule.

constraints: Input order is nondecreasing.
Only the selected pair contributes to the target sum.

items.prompt: Given nonnegative costs in their original order, find the longest contiguous block whose total cost is at most B. A candidate is represented by [left, right], and every cost inside it contributes. Which pattern family matches that candidate?

options.text: Use a two-pointers invariant.
Use a sliding-window validity invariant.
Classify it as two pointers solely because two indices appear.

feedback.reason: The maintained object is the entire contiguous range, so its aggregate validity defines a sliding window.

blocks.text: The task does not ask for two costs that happen to satisfy a relation. It asks for one contiguous block, and adding or removing any interior member changes the block's total. A running sum can be updated when right expands and when left shrinks, so the algorithm maintains the state of [left, right] as one candidate. Nonnegative costs also make budget repair predictable: removing from the left cannot increase the total. If the requirement instead selected two endpoint values and ignored the interior, the candidate would stop being a window and could become a two-pointers relation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_pointers: The two endpoints may look like a pair, but the score depends on all elements between them. Endpoint-only comparison would omit material state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.indices_only: The index count does not classify the algorithm. Here the decisive signal is that [left, right] is the complete candidate whose aggregate is maintained.

constraints: Costs are nonnegative.
The chosen result must preserve original-order contiguity.

items.prompt: Task A asks whether a sorted sequence contains two values with sum T. Task B uses the same sequence but asks for the shortest contiguous segment with sum at least T; all values are positive. Which change is decisive for switching from a pair-search model to a window model?

options.text: Task B makes every element between the boundaries part of the required output.
Both tasks can use variables named left and right.
The sequence is sorted in both tasks.
Both tasks compare a sum with T.

feedback.reason: Task B changes the candidate from two selected values to one contiguous range.

blocks.text: In Task A, the algorithm reasons about a relation between two values; the interior positions are possible future endpoints but are not part of the current candidate. In Task B, the entire interval contributes to the sum and its length is the optimization target, so the maintained state must represent that interval. Positivity supplies the monotone shrink condition needed for a simple variable window. The shared variable names, sortedness, and target value are surface similarities. The output contract is the structural difference that changes the pattern.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_indices: The same names can implement either pattern and therefore cannot decide between them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_input: Sortedness can support pair elimination, but it does not erase Task B's requirement that every interior element belongs to the answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_value: Comparing against a target occurs in both families. What changes is whether two endpoints or an entire range constitute the candidate.

constraints: Task B requires original-order contiguity.
All values are positive.

items.prompt: A loop advances right, adds a[right] to a running total, repeatedly subtracts a[left] while the total exceeds a budget, and records right - left + 1. What is the correct classification?

options.text: Use a two-pointers invariant.
Use a sliding-window validity invariant.
Classify it as two pointers solely because two indices appear.

feedback.reason: Entering and leaving elements update state for the whole contiguous interval.

blocks.text: The algorithm treats [left, right] as one candidate: expansion includes a new member, shrinkage excludes an old member, and the recorded answer is the interval length. Those operations are the signature of a maintained window. The mere presence of two moving indices is not enough to call the algorithm two pointers in the pair-search sense. A two-pointers loop would normally justify one endpoint movement from a relation between endpoint values or from a read/write invariant, without maintaining every interior element as the current candidate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_pointers: This ignores the running state for every member of [left, right]. Endpoint movement is driven by window validity, not by eliminating endpoint pairs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.indices_only: The code does have two indices, but that observation does not identify the invariant or candidate object.

constraints: The running total equals the sum of all elements currently between left and right.
Every array value is nonnegative, so removing a left member cannot increase the running total.

items.prompt: A sorted sequence must yield two positions i < j whose values differ by at most D and whose index gap is at least G. Values strictly between i and j are not aggregated and need not satisfy anything. Which candidate model is structurally correct?

options.text: A relation between the selected endpoints.
A contiguous window containing every position from i through j.
Both models are equivalent because i and j bound a range.

feedback.reason: The constraints are evaluated on the two chosen endpoints, not on all enclosed values.

blocks.text: The index gap mentions the distance between endpoints, but it does not turn the intervening elements into members of the candidate. The maintained decision is still whether a selected pair satisfies two endpoint relations. A contiguous window model would be required if the condition depended on the sum, frequencies, maximum, or another aggregate over every element from i through j. This distinction prevents a common overreach: geometric enclosure by two indices is not the same as semantic ownership of the enclosed range.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.contiguous_window: The endpoints do enclose a span, but the interior is not part of the candidate contract. A window requires the enclosed members to determine validity or score.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_by_notation: The notation is shared, but the models are not equivalent. Candidate membership and the movement invariant determine the pattern.

constraints: Only endpoint values and endpoint indices are tested.
No interior aggregate is part of the requirement.

items.prompt: A task selects two positions whose values satisfy a relation, but the selected positions must be adjacent. Does adjacency alone make the candidate a sliding window?

options.text: No. It remains a pair relation because only the two selected values and their adjacency relation are evaluated; no range-owned aggregate is maintained.
Yes. Any adjacent positions define a sliding window.
No classification is possible because adjacent indices use only one gap.
It becomes a window only after sorting the values.

feedback.reason: Adjacency describes the relation between selected positions; window semantics require ownership of the entire range and its state.

blocks.text: A window can have length two, but the classification comes from the candidate contract, not from geometric adjacency. If the algorithm compares only the two values or their index gap, it is a pair relation. If it maintains a sum, frequencies, maximum, or other property over all positions in a possibly larger interval, it is a window. The minimum candidate size does not erase the invariant distinction.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_by_adjacency: Two adjacent positions form a possible window representation, but no range-owned state is present in the stated task.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_indices_proof: A pair relation can be classified from what its endpoints mean even when their gap is one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_required: Sorting is unrelated to whether the candidate owns the interior range.

constraints: Only the two selected values and their adjacency are scored.

items.prompt: An algorithm maintains a frequency map for all values between left and right and shrinks left until at most K distinct values remain. What fact rules out treating it as a simple endpoint pair?

options.text: The validity and future updates depend on every interior value, so [left, right] is a complete contiguous candidate with range-owned state.
The pair model still applies because the final answer has two endpoints.
The map proves the input must be sorted before either pointer moves.
A frequency map never affects pattern classification.

feedback.reason: The interior frequency state determines validity and must be updated when either boundary moves.

blocks.text: An endpoint pair ignores the values between its positions except as possible future endpoints. Here every value contributes to the distinct-count predicate, so removing a left value changes the candidate state and can restore validity. That expand-and-shrink invariant is sliding-window semantics, regardless of the fact that the answer is eventually reported as a pair of boundaries.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.endpoints_only: The endpoints delimit the candidate, but the interior frequency map is semantically part of that candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_required: Frequency-window validity does not require sorted input; it requires a correctly updated range state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_irrelevant: The map is the evidence that interior elements affect validity and therefore determines the family.

constraints: The answer must be a contiguous subarray of the original sequence.

items.prompt: A sorted pair-sum scan moves the smaller endpoint when the sum is too small. Why is that movement proof different from shrinking a sliding window after its validity predicate fails?

options.text: Pair movement eliminates all remaining pairs using one endpoint, while window shrinking removes range members until the complete candidate becomes valid again.
They are the same proof because both increment left.
A window never has an invalid state; it only expands.
Sortedness makes every shrink operation an endpoint-pair proof.

feedback.reason: The same pointer operation can serve different invariants: discard a set of pair candidates or repair the state of one range candidate.

blocks.text: For sorted pair sum, if left + right is too small, every pair using that left with a right endpoint no larger than the current right is also too small, so left can be discarded from the pair search. For a window, the current range can be invalid and left advances to remove its contribution; the proof concerns the range predicate and the next valid suffix. Direction alone does not identify the family.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_proof: Both increment left but eliminate different candidate sets and maintain different invariants.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_never_rejects: Variable windows commonly expand into invalid states and then shrink until the predicate holds.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_causes_shrink: Sortedness supplies pair elimination only when the pair relation and monotonic comparison support it.

constraints: The pair input is sorted; the window predicate is maintained over the full range.

items.prompt: Select all statements that correctly classify the candidate object in each situation.

options.text: Two selected endpoint values must satisfy a relation, and interior values are irrelevant: pair-relation two pointers.
Every value between boundaries contributes to a distinct-count predicate: sliding window.
Any adjacent pair is automatically a sliding window, even when no interior state exists.
A pair whose endpoints enclose positions is always a range-owned candidate.

feedback.reason: Candidate membership—not the notation [left, right]—determines whether the invariant is pair-based or range-based.

blocks.text: The pair case reasons about two selected positions and a relation between them. The frequency case owns the entire interval and maintains state for every element. A range-shaped notation can describe either; the classification follows which values affect validity, score, and safe movement. This is the core contrast the false heuristic misses.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adjacent_pair_window: Adjacency alone does not make a range aggregate; a length-two pair can remain an endpoint relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_as_geometry_only: Geometric enclosure is not semantic candidate membership. Interior values must matter for window classification.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.pair_endpoints: It identifies the pair candidate and excludes irrelevant interior values.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.range_frequency: It identifies range-owned state and validity repair.

constraints: More than one statement is correct.

items.prompt: A prompt mentions left and right but does not say whether interior elements affect the answer. What clarification is most important before selecting a pattern?

options.text: Ask whether the candidate is only the two selected positions or the entire contiguous interval and its aggregate state.
Count the indices and choose the family with the matching number of variables.
Assume a window because every left/right pair spans an interval.
Assume two pointers because a window is only a special name for two pointers.

feedback.reason: The missing candidate contract is exactly the distinction between endpoint relation and range-owned state.

blocks.text: If only the endpoints are selected, movement must be justified by a pair relation such as sorted elimination. If every element between them contributes, the algorithm needs a window state and a validity update. Without this information, variable names and pointer count cannot determine the pattern. Asking the contract first prevents an implementation template from replacing problem analysis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.count_indices: Both families commonly use two indices, so count provides no classification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.assume_window: A span is not a window unless its interior is the maintained candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.assume_pair: A window is not merely a cosmetic label; its range-owned state creates different proof obligations.

constraints: The output contract is intentionally incomplete until candidate membership is clarified.
